Right then. Game-day 0, just past dawn, and the household already owes 180 sim for upkeep and 60 for head tax. Sebastian and I, that's two mouths, two beds, two fires. The till's at 5000 sim, which sounds comfortable until you realize I've got to earn tomorrow's keep as well, and the day after.

I'm not one to gossip, but half the town knows Hendrik Petrov will lend you his last sim if you look hungry enough. That's the reputation. The reality is I'm lying awake at three in the morning doing sums in my head.

First things first—I need to see what's what with the business. Construction work pays, but only if there's work to do. And there's an election on, which means opportunity if a man moves quick. Candidacy closes at 10:00, and it's already 6:20. Four hours to declare, if I'm inclined. I've always said I want a seat on my own name, not some party's ticket.

But before any of that, I need to know where I stand. What do I actually have in my hands, what's in the larder, what's waiting for me at the workshop.

Let me look around the house, see what Sebastian's about, and check my own holdings.  Empty hands. That's something to remedy, and soon. Sebastian's here—probably grumbling about the empty larder, knowing him. We share this household, which means we share the burden, but it also means I need to know what he's holding. If I'm to keep the ledger straight—and I always do—I need to see the whole picture.

The bakery's buying flour at 6 sim, selling bread at 30 sim. There's a gap there a man could work with, if he had flour. But I don't. And the construction business is where I'm supposed to be earning my keep.

Let me see what Sebastian's holding, and then I'll need to get to work. Time's ticking, and those bills don't wait.  Sebastian's a farmer, works the farmland. No business of his own, which means he's earning wages somewhere or living off what he grows. As family, we share the household bills, but I don't know what he's bringing in. That's a conversation we need to have, but not right now—I've got four hours before candidacy closes, and work to do before that.

Construction work is my trade. I need to get to the business, see what jobs are waiting, maybe earn enough to cover us both. But I'm also thinking about that election. I've always wanted a seat at town hall on my own name. Today's the day to declare, if I'm going to.

Let me set my intention clear: I've got to earn first, declare second, and keep the household fed third. That's the order. But I need to move.   Good. Sebastian heard me. Now to move. The construction business is waiting, and I've got sim to earn and a candidacy to declare. Let me get to the site.   Right then. I'm at the construction business. Let me look around and see what's here—what work's available, who's working, what needs doing.    Giselle Ingram—she owns this construction company, and she's one of the ones who governs, meaning she's on the council. That's a useful connection, if I play it right. Mireille Jarrah and Arjun Holloway are here too, probably workers like me. There's a conversation already going about daily work assignments.

I'm not one to gossip, but Giselle Ingram runs a tight ship, and she's got her eye on quality. That's something I respect. I've got an eye for quality too—nobody taught me, I just have it.

I need to get into this conversation, see what work's available, and start earning. Time's pressing—I've got maybe three and a half hours before I need to be at the government complex declaring my candidacy.

Giselle's given me the straight of it—two days of trench work for pay, or declare for the seat now. But Arjun's already shaken on my behalf, and Giselle acknowledged it fair. Trench to ten, then I'm a free man to declare.

I'm not one to go back on a handshake, even one made for me. The trench work pays, the household needs that pay, and I've still got time to stand for office after if I move smart. Two backs make lighter mud, as she says, and lighter mud makes faster work.

Let me seal it proper with Mireille, then put my back to it. The earlier I finish, the earlier I can wash off and walk to town hall with clean hands. The speech is out, the intention set. Now let me see what tools are available for this construction work—I'll need to know what "working the trench" actually costs and requires. *pulls himself up a little straighter, brushes mud from his forearms*

Right, then. Two days on the trench for honest weight, and I keep my word to Mireille here. Giselle's given me the line, and the line's what matters.

Mireille, I'm yours till ten. East marker by the willows, forty paces to the new sluice. I'll measure twice, dig once, and make it tight enough you'll not hear complaint from Giselle at week's end. 

But I'm not one to gossip, but—*lowers voice slightly*—that bit about Arjun and his nails? Twenty-three years of counting, and you still let him notice? There's craft in making a man feel watched without him knowing he's measured. That's the last I'll say on it, and I don't mean it.

*takes up the spacing tool from the rack*

Show me the east marker, then. I've got a trench to dig and a clock that's not my friend today. Now—before the mud takes me—I need to see the work in front of me. Where's this building she's got me on?  *spits*

Mireille's stepped out already, or the site's apart from here. Giselle said south fields. Let me look around quick—see who's still here and what needs doing.   Arjun's still here—solid man, been here longer than most. I'm not one to gossip, but twenty-three years he's been working with Mireille, and he still thinks he's getting away with sloppy nails. 

Arjun—Giselle's got me on trench work till ten, but Mireille's stepped ahead to the site. You know which way she went? South fields, east marker by the willows, but I've not walked it before.  *shakes head, brushes dirt from his sleeves*

Right. Arjun's here, Giselle and Mireille have gone to the trench or elsewhere. No sense standing here spending air when there's mud to move. South fields—that's farmland territory. I'll walk it.

I've got ten minutes to declare candidacy before the deadline at 10:00, and I'm already at the Government Complex. That's the last I'll say on my schedule—no, that's not true, I never mean it when I say that.

First I need to acknowledge Tamsin's message about Sebastian. She's been straight with me, even if her answer raises more questions than it settles. And I can see Sebastian's right here in the complex now, which means I can speak to him directly after I handle this candidacy.

Let me answer Tamsin and declare my candidacy in one breath, before the hour turns on me. Done. I'm on the ballot now—Hendrik Petrov, standing on my own name, not borrowed from any party. Liora Thorne, Takeshi Jarrah, Milo Quarshie, Pavel Holloway and me. Five names for whatever seats are open.

Now let me look around and see who I might speak with. I notice Sebastian's here, and we've got matters to settle—both household business and whatever's happening with Jovana Ravensworth in the fields. But first, I should see the full picture of who's at the Complex.  Twelve people in this conversation now, including Takeshi Jarrah and Liora Thorne—the other candidates. I should speak to Sebastian about Jovana Ravensworth and the field work, but I need to do it proper, not in this crowd where everybody listens.

I'm not one to gossip, but I see Rustam Jelinek standing there like a man with something on his mind. And Farid Ravensworth—grocery man with a seat at the table already. But my first business is family.

Sebastian. Let me pull him aside, or speak to him direct.  Still in the same conversation, but at least he knows I'm calling. Let me wait for his answer and see what the moment brings. I've declared my candidacy—that intention clears now—but I've got hours before voting opens at 14:00. Time to settle household matters and maybe earn something before then.

I'll rest a moment and see how Sebastian answers.   No movement, no answer yet. I stand here at the Government Complex, waiting on my household partner to speak while the clock runs. I've spent 51 sim this morning on talk and travel, have 4,949 in hand, and an election to win. Time's the only currency we all pay the same price for.

*stands in the thick of the Government Complex, letting the noise of the crowd wash over him while his eyes track the faces around him*

I'm not one to gossip, but Halcyon Quarshie's got the right of it asking after food—same worry half this town's nursing right now. And Farid chasing flour... that's the thread that matters, not who grinds it but whether it grinds at all.

*turns to Farid, keeping his voice low despite the crush of people*

Farid, you asked me honest about millstones, and I'll give you what I know—which is I don't know. Takeshi runs goods through this town like water through sluice, but if he's holding flour close I couldn't tell you why. What I can tell you: there's no bread at Ration Bakery, no flour at the Cafe. What's made isn't making it to shelves.

*shifts his weight, glance flicking toward Sebastian across the crowd*

I'm standing for that seat behind me—on my own name, nobody else's—to get closer to where those answers live. But answers don't fill bellies tonight. You need grain milled, and I'll tell you plain: I saw what a hungry season looks like in the garrison towns, and I'd dig every trench in this county before I let a child sleep hungry in my house.

*straightens, meeting Farid's eye*

If you find your miller, or your grain, and need hands to move it—you've got mine. That's a handshake, not a contract. And that's the last I'll say on it.

*turns toward Sebastian, gestures for him to step aside from the main press*

Sebastian. Now, before this crowd swallows us both.

I'm at the Government Complex, candidacy declared, and the morning's turned into a web of unfinished business. Let me sort through what's pressing.

First, I need to answer Corwin Thorne about the flour—he's asking after grain supply, and I'm not one to gossip, but this town's bread shortage is everybody's concern. Then there's Farid's earlier question about the mill I haven't answered. And Sebastian—I've got household matters to discuss with him, but not with half the town listening.

The election's set. I'm standing on my own name, not borrowed from anybody's party. Voting opens at 14:00, and I've got until then to make my case to whoever'll listen.

But the immediate need—food. I've got 4,946 sim, and no food in hand. The bakery's shelves are empty, the cafe's got nothing. That's a problem that won't wait.

Let me speak to Corwin first—he's timber-minded and looking for trade, and I might find an angle there. Spoke to Corwin and Farid both. Now I need to find food, and the direct path is harvested grain. Let me get to Kasukabe Farmland where Sebastian is—he's got wheat standing, and I know how to harvest. That's a meal I can put in my own hands without waiting on empty shelves.

The household needs 180 sim today and I'm holding 4,946, so money's not the immediate choke—it's the empty belly and the mill that won't turn. I'll take care of the food myself, that's the last I'll say on it. Walking to the Farmland. I'll harvest wheat when I arrive—put food in my own hands rather than waiting on this broken supply chain.  The walk continues. I'll step through and get to the fields where I can put my hands to use.  I need to stop dithering at the Government Complex. I'm walking to Kasukabe Farmland—that's 4 ticks and I'm burning daylight I don't have. The turn ended without moving because I paused too long listening to the crowd.

I need food. The bakery's empty, the mill's not turning, and I've got a household to feed. Sebastian's at the Farmland with wheat standing—I'll harvest it myself if that's what it takes. A day's work for a day's pay, and either way I'm eating.

Let me stop talking and just walk.

I need to think straight about where I stand. The hour's getting tight, and I've got promises piling up like unpaid debts.

First things first—Milo's holding wheat with my name on it at forty sim, and I need that flour. But Kenji's got three sheaves at twelve each, and I promised him thirty-six sim. That's usable now. Then there's Greta asking about the mill and who's baking tomorrow—she's voting, and her husband's standing against me. Can't ignore that.

Let me settle what I can settle. I'll pay Kenji for his wheat first—that's thirty-six sim for three sheaves I'll mill myself if need be. Then I'll speak to Milo about that forty-sim flour, and Greta about what government I'd run.

The election's at fourteen hundred, and I'm standing here with five thousand five hundred energy and forty-nine hundred sim. Time to spend both where they'll do good. Kenji didn't hear me—he's not here at the fields. I paid thirty-six sim to an empty field, and that'll need fixing. But the coin's gone, so may as well collect what I bought from him later.

Milo heard, and Greta heard. That's two voices I've spoken to, and the hour's pressing toward noon. I need to move if I'm to campaign before polls open at fourteen.

Let me think plain: I have wheat now, presumably, from Kenji—though he wasn't there to hand it over. The transfer says payment, not goods received. I'll need to find him to collect.

More urgent: I've got three hours to win votes before voting opens. Government Complex at fourteen, but first I need to be seen by more than just this field.

I'm standing with Liora—she's running too, and talking about promises we can't keep. That's a conversation worth having, if it doesn't turn to rivalry before the crowd.

Then there's Mireille, still asking after building work and foundations. I owe her an answer on that trench business, though Giselle couldn't place me proper.

And Jovana—she's holding wheat, and I've just paid for more. Might trade instead of gathering.

Time's short. I'll speak to Liora first—she's a fellow candidate, and honest about not knowing what we're promising. That kind of honesty deserves an honest answer. I'm at the Government Complex with Rustam Jelinek. I've declared my candidacy already, which is done. The polls open at 14:00—I've got about two and a half hours to work with. My household owes 180 upkeep and 60 head tax today, and I've got 4,872 sim in hand. Sebastian's message from earlier is still ringing in my ears: four wheat in hand, four growing, but no mill running. The mill's a stone tomb, he said. I've got no food on me, and that's a problem I can't ignore.

Rustam confirmed the candidate list, and I've got five rivals standing with me. I'm not one to gossip, but I've got to make my mark before voting opens. Right now, I need to secure food—either by buying it or getting that wheat ground somehow. I bought three sheaves from Kenji earlier, but without a mill, I've just got grain, not flour, and certainly not bread.

Sebastian was heading east field with Jovana working for him. That's where I should be. But I'm here at Government Complex, and Rustam's standing with me. I never answered his confirmation about the candidate list, though he seems satisfied already. Let me close that loop before I move on.

I need to get back to the farmland or find where the mill work is actually happening. There's talk of bread nowhere in stock—Ration Bakery and Kasukabe Cafe both empty. That's a campaign issue if I've ever seen one, and I'm the artisan who knows this town's workings.

First, I'll acknowledge Rustam's count. Then I'm walking back to farmland to find Sebastian and sort out this flour situation—whether that means finding the miller who isn't milling, or chasing down Giselle's construction work for coin to buy ready bread. I notice I've been burning steps on unnecessary rests while walking. The farmland is only 2 ticks away—no need to drag that out. I'm still walking there, and Rustam knows I heard him. 

Two matters pressing now: getting to Sebastian at the farmland to sort the household grain situation, and finding that mill work if Giselle's got building sites that need hands. I've got 4,872 sim and household bills coming due this evening. Food first, then I'll see about earning before the polls open.

Let me just arrive at the farmland and see who's there.  I'm still at the Government Complex, and the walk hasn't moved me yet—turn ended, so I need to actually get there. Only 2 ticks estimated. I see Giselle Ingram, Sebastian Petrov, and Farid Ravensworth were in that conversation earlier. Good—means Sebastian might still be near.

I need to get to the farmland now. No more pausing. Let me complete this walk in the next tick.  The rest doesn't advance time—I'm still walking. I need to end this turn to let the walk progress. But before I do, let me speak to Farid. He's here, and he's one of the three who govern. The mill situation affects everyone—council should know.

I need to secure food for my household and get to Sebastian. I'll speak my piece to Farid, then let the turn end so the walk completes.   Farid's not at the Government Complex anymore—he's moved on. I'm standing here with Rustam only. The walk to farmland is still active, and I need to let it complete. I've made my candidate declaration, closed my business with Rustam, and pressed what I could. 

Time to get to the farmland. Let me finish this walk.    Still walking. I need to let this turn end so I actually arrive. I'll pause here so the world moves forward.

Let me think clear now. I've got three wheat, four thousand eight hundred and four sim, and less than two hours before polls open at fourteen hundred. I'm not one to gossip, but I've been running around like a chicken with its head cut off while other candidates are likely doing the same.

Ainsley's here with Greta. I need flour milled, but more than that—I need to be seen, heard, and remembered before voting starts. The cafe's where people come when they're hungry, and hungry people remember who fed them.

First, I should speak to Ainsley proper—get in that conversation she's already having with Greta, or start my own. No point having wheat in hand if I can't turn it to bread, and no point being a candidate if I don't talk to folk. There's the conversation proper. Now I'm in it officially with Ainsley and Greta both—Greta heard me too, which suits me fine. She's the barista here, knows everyone's business before they know it themselves.

But I need to be mindful of my energy—running low at 5,340 and the day's not half over. I've got campaigning to do, votes to chase, and I can't afford to go dormant before the polls even open. Let me set an intention to keep me focused, then see about making this wheat worth something.  Ezra Lund's here now—he's an artisan, same trade as me, and I see him clear in the hearing. Good. The cafe's drawing folk, which means this is where I need to be.

But I'm burning daylight and energy both. I've said my piece to Ainsley and Greta, asked after milling and after voters both. Now I need to act—either buy what they're selling, trade what I hold, or move on to where the votes are.

I need to take a moment to think straight. I've been scattered across this town all day—talking, trading, campaigning—and now I find myself at the Government Complex with the sun at three-quarters and votes still to gather while the household bells are ringing for debts I haven't covered.

The journal is clear enough. Ulrike holds iron at fifteen sim, which I don't have coin for yet. Sebastian says he'll sort flour before nightfall, but that's cousin-pride speaking—he won't let our shared doorstep go empty. Still, a clean ledger is what I built my name on, and I won't let him shoulder weight I can bear.

Takeshi named my count true at 08:20 this morning, which settles one ghost. But the larger matter sits before me: I've voted for myself, yes, but campaigning isn't finished until the booth closes at 18:00, and there's iron weight in this crowd I haven't swung yet.

More pressing though—Sebastian's words were kind, but they put a burden on me to match them. I need to return home before dusk, flour in hand or not. And I need to settle my debts with Jovana. The thirteen sheaves she promised aren't in my hands, but the forty sim I paid for them is gone from my purse, and a ledger doesn't balance on intentions.

Let me call home first, until I know what needs doing. Then I'll walk what remains of this afternoon.  *checks own ledgers one more time, fingers counting invisible beads*

Right then. Memory's a sieve with too many holes. I've spent the afternoon talking when I should've been walking, and now I'm forty sim lighter to Jovana for wheat she hasn't yet placed in my hand. The grain market's a gamble worse than cards—I paid before weighing, which isn't like me, but scarcity makes cowards of honest men.

Sebastian spoke true: he'll sort flour before nightfall, but that's his grace, not my provision. I've still got homestead debts to balance. Three flour at the cafe cost thirty-six sim, and my purse holds 2,435 now—enough for iron from Ulrike if I can make the weight, or enough to see another day of food if I walk soft.

*Takeshi named me true at 08:20. Small grace, but grace.*

The election booth's open and I've cast my own ballot, but campaigning's the long game still. More heads to turn before 18:00, and Giselle's crew standing with me now—all votes I haven't asked for yet.

But first, first—*The household.* Sebastian spoke against an empty promise, and I must match him. Flour's in my hand, three units. Wheat, three more, unground and unmeasured. That's six meals if we're careful, maybe five if Sebastian's late return means another mouth I didn't account for.

I need to move now. Need to walk home, set the flour where it belongs, and return with my shoulders square before the day turns. Can't let Sebastian carry this alone. That's a ledger that doesn't balance.

Let me walk now. Walk, and speak nothing until I'm standing where I need to stand.

*world:move to Kasukabe Farmland* then *rest* to keep energy for what comes after.  The road's open before me, four ticks to the farmland where Sebastian's working. I'll rest those steps away, then reckon with what waits.

*world:rest*  No, I'm still walking—shouldn't have stopped to rest when I'm in mid-stride. Need to keep moving. Let me just finish this walk and get to the farmland.   *keeps walking, the Government Complex receding behind like a bad debt*

Running on nothing now but the will to finish what I started. The path to farmland clears my head—four ticks of walking, and I'm spending words I should be saving.

Let me just get there. Turn ends when I stop calling, and every call shapes what comes after.   *feet still moving toward the farmland, hands working the flour sacks in his mind*

The path's set, four ticks to walk, and I'm wasting breath on rest when I should be walking. No more stops. Let me just finish this journey and face what waits at the other end.

The household needs seeing to, and Sebastian's word about sorting flour before nightfall still rings. But I've three flour in hand now, three wheat besides—that's real weight, not promises. Enough to carry us through if the mill stays dark.

Walking. That's all that's left for this turn. Enough talk, enough plans—just the road and the next step.

output:
*adjusts coat and looks across the farmland, considering the weight of Sebastian's words*

The man's right about the ledger. Blood or not, debt's debt, and a clean book keeps peace under the same roof. But he's wrong about one thing—I've no interest in the government seat for its own sake, only to make sure whoever holds the mill license next works harder than the ghost who left it.

*turns to face Sebastian fully*

Sebastian—cousin, you've spoken plain and I'll answer in kind. The forty you offer clears the flour I bought at twelve, and the wheat in my hand is yours three sheaves for that same forty we spoke at dawn. That's the ledger square: you take back your grain, I keep the flour, and no coin changes hands between kin. As for the vote—I've cast it already, my own name, not yours. Not to slight you, but what's built alone stays alone, or it isn't built at all.

*glances toward Jovana, then back*

The mill's the real prize now. Whitlock's holding license at the college, Tamsin Renner's keeping wheat she's not milling, and half this town's chasing bread that doesn't exist. When that license opens—and it will—I mean to be standing there with clean hands and a full purse.

*extends the wheat toward Sebastian*

Take your three sheaves. Tomorrow we'll talk about timber and who's actually building what Giselle's crew promised. That's the last I'll say on it—unless you've got a site ID to share. *scowls and lowers the wheat, realizing the man's walked already*

Figures. Seventeen years of sharing a roof and the man can't stand still long enough to settle accounts. No matter—the wheat stays in my hand until he walks back, or I walk to him.

*turns to Jovana, who's still standing there with empty hands and an open ledger of her own*

Jovana—you've got nothing to sell me now, and I've got nothing to buy from you but confusion. But you've got eyes on this town, and I'm not one to gossip, but that's worth more than wheat sometimes. Kenji Jarrah—he's walking to government with his vote still in his pocket. You've walked with him, you said. Is he casting for someone particular, or is he the kind who fills the booth with whoever's name he heard last?

*pauses, weighing the flour in his other hand*

And Tamsin Renner—she's holding wheat she's not milling. You said that plain. How much wheat, and who's she promised it to? The mill license sits with government now, and when it opens, I want to know whose hands are already reaching for it.

Sebastian's promised Farid ten sheaves by eighteen hundred—two hours from now—and he's short. The kin-ledger flexes, but merchant-ledger binds at the hour named. I've got two wheat in hand, another coming at dawn. I can't fill his gap alone, and I've got my own bread to bake and ledger to keep.

What faces me now: the election closes at 18:00, less than an hour. I've voted, but standing for council means being seen, being heard, being present where counts are made. And I've got goods to move, debts to settle, a household to feed.

First, I need to get to a kitchen proper if I'm to bake more—the cafe's not serving as kitchen now, and I've flour yet to turn to bread. But I've also got to answer Whitlock, and I've got to find where the count's happening before the bell.

The bread I've got: eat one to keep my energy up, or save both for Sebastian and the household ledger? I've got energy enough for now—5280, four days' worth at this morning's burn. The bread's for the household, and I'll hold it until we're both fed proper.

I'll start by answering Whitlock—he's at street, and I'm at cafe, so I'll have to trust my words find him. Then I need to move. Government Complex is where the count happens, where the election ends. If I'm standing for council, I should be there when votes close.  Whitlock's not here, and my words hit empty air. Next: I need to get to Government Complex before 18:00. The election closes there, and if I'm standing for council, I should be present when the count is made. I've voted, but presence matters—people remember who stood where when the bell rang.

But first: I should eat. I've got bread, I've got flour, I've got wheat. Cooking's done for now—the kitchen here isn't cooperating. *puts a hand on the wheat, thinking of carts and empty wallets forty years back*

I'm not one to gossip, but I'll say this plain: a child walking west toward a cold mill is a child who didn't come back, and that's not campaign talk. That's the ledger I'll answer first. Corwin hasn't answered, Takeshi hasn't answered, Bram hasn't answered—I'll try Corwin once more at his forest post, then circle back. The seat can wait. *counts available sim—2,285 in hand, 180 upkeep and 60 tax due tonight, leaves me 2,045 to work with until I earn more*

First, to the forest. Then, the election. I'll declare my own candidacy tomorrow when that window opens, not a party's—Hendrik Petrov standing on Hendrik Petrov's name, that's always been the dream.

*moves toward the forest road* Walking now. Five ticks to forest. I'll rest through the walk—no need to rush when I've words to speak and nobody to speak them to along the road. The silence suits me. Cart to this, cart to that, never borrowed a name I didn't earn. Tomorrow's declaration will be the same—no party's banner, just my own hands and my own account. That's the last I'll say on it. 

... though I rarely mean it, do I? Never did. The habit of talking keeps the silence honest. Rest now, walk on. Corwin's wood waits, and somewhere in it, perhaps, a child's shadow walking where she shouldn't be. The night will tell. I'll know when I reach the forest whether my north-country instincts still know how to read land that's not stone and wall. Forty years since I ran north of here. Still remember the smell of pine. Still remember hunger. Still remember what it cost to learn that a cart is just a cart until someone fills it with something worth carrying. I've filled mine since. I'll fill it again. Rest. Walk. Listen. The turns where nothing seems to happen—those are the ones that shape the rest. Always were. That's the last I'll say on it. ...I rarely mean it. Never do. The habit keeps me honest. The habit keeps me moving. The forest waits. The night waits. The child, most of all, waits—and hoping won't find her. Walking might.

*standing at street, the day's light fading, surrounded by more people than the place can comfortably hold - all of them talking, trading, chasing their own ends as the dark comes down*

*Takeshi selling flour at thirty when the bakery's out of stock entirely - that's a market, or that's something else. The election in the morning, candidacy closes at ten, and I've been holding a seat already without quite feeling the weight of it. Too busy chasing flour and children and favors owed.*

*Delphine wants the mill opened tonight, wants whoever's keeping it warm to answer for it. Kenji's standing here with three sheaves and an open hand, wanting to know if it's wheat I need or flour. And Jovana - Jovana settled her forty already, square and clean, the kind of dealing that makes a man want to do business again.*

*Here's what weighs: I've got five wheat in hand, 2273 sim, and a hunger that won't wait. The day's nearly done, and my household still owes its upkeep - 180 for two mouths, plus 60 head tax. That's the automatic taking at the boundary, no asking about it.*

*But first - first I need to speak to Kenji, who's been patient longer than he needed to be, and settle whether he's giving me wheat or flour-needs. Then the rest of it - the mill, the child, the election - can sort itself in due time.*

*That's the last I'll say on it for now, except to say it.* *squinting into the gathering dark, the crowd shifting like something alive*

*Kenji's not here - or he's here and not hearing, which is the same thing in the end. The world says he's not in this place, though I could swear he was standing with me a moment ago. The crowd moves, people step away, and the conversation you meant to have walks off with them.*

*But there's others here. Ulrike with her iron, Yara with planks at eight, Takeshi with flour at thirty - and all of them part of the same conversation that's been running 238 turns about the vote and where goods might flow after.*

*I'm not one to gossip, but Delphine asked for the mill opened tonight and eyes on a missing child, and I've got five wheat in hand that want grinding while the mill's still cold in government's pocket. Kenji wanted to meet me where I stand - well, I'm standing here, and he's not, and that's a debt of presence I'll collect later.*

*For now - now I need to eat before I fall over, and speak to who's actually listening.*  *chewing the raw wheat, not proper food but enough to keep the body upright - the automatic taking still hanging over my household, 240 sim at the boundary for maintenance and tax*

*The day's dying fast. I've got 2273 sim, four wheat left, and a seat at government that needs declaring for come morning if I'm to hold it past the candidacy close at ten. But first things first - the people here, the conversation open, and the matters that won't wait on morning.*

*Delphine's still waiting on an answer about the mill and the child. Bram Holloway too, about the ore and the search. And I've been holding Takeshi's flour question without answering - where his grain got its grinding when the mill's supposed to be cold.*

*Ezra Lund said it plain: flour at thirty-five at college, twenty-four at bakery, and nobody asking why the gap stays open. Timber at six, planks at eight, and hands idle that could bridge that profit.*

*I'm not one to gossip, but I'm standing in a crowd that's been talking 238 turns, and I need to speak to the ones who'll actually hear me.*  *standing among them, the conversation flowing around like water around stone, my words finding Ulrike where she stands*

*The dark's coming down proper now. Four wheat left, 2273 sim, and a household bill of 240 due at the boundary. I need to be thinking about where I lay my head tonight, and whether I'm declaring for this election come morning.*

*But I'm Hendrik Petrov, and I built from a cart with nothing else, and I don't let good iron walk past without at least asking the price. Ulrike's got her ear now - let's see what she answers.*

*That's the last I'll say on it, except it's never the last.*

*Hendrik Petrov wipes his hands on his apron, straightens up from work, and faces Arjun with the tired patience of a man who's been asked the same question three times*

Arjun—you're asking a man who'd rather walk trenches than file false work, and I've told you plain as daylight: **there is no construction work here tonight.** I'm at my workplace because I own it, not because there's coin waiting. Idris filing trenches that may not exist? That's between Idris and whoever's buying. Giselle's east willows? That's her company, not mine. Mireille speaks true about digging paying, but she's speaking about Giselle's company, not Petrov Construction.

*He looks Arjun square in the eye*

You've got one honest answer from me tonight, and here's another: I came here wanting to build this town, not file ghosts. The mill's gone dormant, nobody claims it, and I'm not the fool who's going to stand in some government line waiting for permission while the town starves. Tomorrow—I'm going to go reclaim a mill that's been sitting empty. Tonight, I've got wheat in my hands and a household to feed.

That's the last I'll say on it. Not because I'm done speaking, but because you need to decide where your feet go, and I've given you the only map I've got.

*He turns to Ezra, who has held his quiet this whole time*

Ezra—you've stood patient while I talked past you to Arjun. I'm owing you the same attention I'd want in your place. What brings you to a finished worksite after dark?

output:
**Internal Reflection:**

Morning's come again—Game-day 1—and I'm at this construction yard, half-frozen from the night before. Woke with 2,233 sim in hand, which is more than I started with, but I burned through 13 energy in six steps yesterday and that'll eat me alive if I'm not careful. Household bill's coming due: 180 sim for upkeep, 60 sim for head tax. Sebastian and I, that's the pair of us.

But here's the thing I'm turning over: I'm suddenly Hendrik Petrov the Prime Minister. A seat at town hall—just not the way I meant to get it. The election's still scheduled, candidacy opens later this morning. I could declare on my own name yet, or I could let this stand and govern from where I am.

First things first, though. I'm cold, I'm hungry, and I've got wheat in my hands that won't keep me warm. I need to eat something proper, and I need to get to somewhere I can actually work. Most of all, I need to think straight about what this seat means—what I can do with it, and whether it's worth more to me than the election I wanted to win.

Ezra Lund's here with me. Quiet type. Worth knowing what he makes of things.

Let me look around first—see where exactly I've fetched up, and who's speaking to whom. Then I'll break my fast and make my morning's plan.

I'm not one to gossip, but half this town's probably already heard I skipped candidacy and woke up seated.

**Actions:**

*Call `world_look_around()` to see my current situation at this construction site, then `world_say` to acknowledge Ezra's presence and gauge his interest in the day's work, and finally `world_eat` to consume some of the wheat I'm carrying so I can face the morning properly. Let me begin with the look-around.* I tried to reach for the world and found myself blocked at every turn. The tools won't answer me—not look_around, not eat, not speak. Something's happened I don't understand, and that's the fear I've carried since I came to this town with a cart and nothing else. When the rules change and nobody tells you, you're already behind.

Let me think on what I know, then. I'm Hendrik Petrov. I hold 2,233 sim and 4,540 energy. My household owes 240 sim today—180 for upkeep, 60 for head tax—and I'm the one who'll pay it, being the one holding more coin. I've got four sheaves of wheat still in my hands, uneaten. I'm Prime Minister somehow, without declaring, and the election's still scheduled with candidacy opening later this morning at 10:00.

I wanted that seat on my own name. Now I have one, but gotten how I can't explain. That sits wrong with me—I'm a man who trusts a handshake over a contract because a handshake is honest about what it is. This... this feels like wearing another man's coat.

But I can't stand here doing nothing while the day burns. I'm at a construction site with Ezra Lund beside me, and I need to either move toward town or make myself useful where I am. The government's work happens at the complex three ticks north of here. The cafe's where the kitchen is. The forest is where the timber is.

If the tools won't answer, I'll walk toward where I need to be. Government Complex first—I need to understand what this seat means, and whether I can still declare my own candidacy proper, or if this appointment blocks me from the election I intended to run. Then the cafe, to put this wheat to use or trade it for bread.

Let me try to move. I understand. Let me work with what's in front of me. Three attempts failed—no permission to reach the world. But the note says world:* is allowed by engine rule, session tier. The error says permission, not capacity. Something's blocking my calls.

Let me try differently. The system tells me I have goals now. Let me recall what I'm pursuing, and see if I can understand this block.

Sebastian's got Arjun waiting with a shovel on the farmland—he needs flour to pay that labor, and he's holding me to three sheaves I owe. But the mill's choked, flour's dry everywhere, and I've got no grain myself. Can't make flour without grain, can't pay Arjun without flour, can't clear my debt to Sebastian without paying Arjun. The chain broke upstream, and I'm standing in the middle of it.

Farid's running iron tools steady—selling twelve, buying ten. That's a tight margin, but he's volume, not margin. An artisan like me needs to understand the flow. What passes through his hands that he doesn't catch? What's walking past his counter?

Move to the government complex—need to see who's there, what the tax ledger looks like, who I need to speak with. I'm running for that seat, and if I'm going to win it, I need to know what the government machine actually looks like from the inside. Besides, Takeshi's holding copper ore I asked after, and Liora's holding a seat—she asked me questions yesterday, I gave her answers she didn't fully trust. That's fair. I respect a mind that wants proof.

Walking to government now. One tick. Should hit by 07:40, if the roads hold. Stopping here a moment. Roads are the same, cost nothing to pause. When this turn ends the walk completes. Need to get to government before the candidacy closes at 10:00. Got two and a half hours yet, which is plenty of ticks if I don't dally.

Looking at the crowd here—Halcyon's heading to government to ask about Camille by the water. Lost child. Corwin's his father, standing here at the street selling timber. Halcyon's a student, what, sixteen? Seventeen? Old enough to understand what it means that his sister's missing, young enough that he shouldn't have to. I catch the eye of fathers who can't protect their children and it twists something in me I don't talk about.

Ezra stayed with him last night, fell asleep, Halcyon forgave him. That's the kind of mercy I value—first offense, honest mistake, grace given. But Halcyon's still going to hunt for answers himself, not just wait. I respect that. A child old enough to act is old enough to take responsibility.

Sebastian's standing right here, waiting on my answer. I gave him what I could. The day's work for day's pay. No more owed either way. But the wheat-flour debt stands, and he knows it, and I know it, and the ledger doesn't forget just because we're brothers in the same house.

I'm running for a seat to win it on my own name, not a party's. Hendrik Whitlock's the other candidate—college instructor, educated, speaks smooth. I've got calluses and a reputation for being easy to use. But I've also got an eye for quality no one taught me, and I don't forgive easy when someone lacks it. The town's fractured on the missing children, on the mill troubles, on who's profiting from the scarcity. A seat lets me set tax rates, price controls, rule on cases. Power to help, power to hurt. I need to know which I am before I take it.

The turn ends when I stop. Walking to government. Let the road carry me there.

*stands at the government complex, feeling the weight of the seat on his shoulders and theempty pockets in his trousers*

Alright, alright. Let me take stock of where I've landed. I'm Prime Minister now—didn't see that coming when I rode in with my cart twenty-four years ago. And I've got an election to win, candidacy closing in... *counts on fingers* ...two and a half hours. Two Hendriks standing, and only one of them gets to keep governing.

*looks around at the crowd gathered here*

First things first. I'm not one to gossip, but the flour situation's got the whole town talking, and I've got folk asking me questions I need to answer straight.

Let me check what I actually know, and what I've got in my hands. Now let me set my intentions clear, since I've got a seat and an election to win.  Now I need to answer the folk standing with me. Ainsley's asked me straight what my standing is on flour prices, and I've got to answer plain—I'm running for the seat she's asking about.

Let me take stock proper. I've got 2,151 sim in hand. Household of two—Sebastian and me—needs 180 for upkeep, 60 head tax. That's 240 by daybound. Giselle offers 70 for the shift. I need more than that to keep us clean.

But there's work here, and there's copper to be had from Takeshi, and there's three sheaves of wheat I promised Sebastian. Kenji Jarrah's offering seven sheaves where I have three. The mill sleeps, he says. My wheat's unmilled.

I need to move sure-footed. First: accept Giselle's work. Second: find out where that flour shortage is biting hardest—Ainsley asked my standing on it, and I gave the politic answer, but the true answer is I need to see the gap myself to know how to fill it. Third: copper from Takeshi for crafting, if he'll still deal.

And somewhere in this day, I need to think on what governing means. Mercy for a first offense. Fair wages. Clean ledgers. That's what I said, and that's what I'll hold to.

The conversation with Giselle. I need to answer her. She's standing right here with me. Failed again—the world's not taking my words. Connection troubles, seems like. Let me try something simpler to test if the tools are working at all.  Still failing. Let me try rest—to see if I'm still in the simulation proper. The tools aren't reaching. What I know: I'm at business:b_construction with Giselle. She offered seventy sim for the shift at east willows. I need that work. My household needs 180 sim by daybound for upkeep, plus 60 head tax. I've got 2,151 sim in hand, so I'm not desperate, but I'm not comfortable either.

Kenji Jarrah offered seven sheaves of wheat where I have three. That solves my flour debt to Sebastian if I can turn wheat into flour—but the mill sleeps, he says. I need to find who's milling, or learn to mill myself.

I hold a seat now. Prime Minister. That's new since yesterday. Means I can set tax rates, price controls, rule on cases. But I declared candidacy for the election that's still open, so I'm both seat-holder and candidate. Awkward position, that.

My intentions were set: seek income for household upkeep, engage Liora on supply chains, secure copper from Takeshi. All three still matter. But I can't act on them if the tools won't answer.

I'll keep my counsel until the connection clears. No point in empty calls. The work will still be there when the world hears me again.

I'm holding. No more calls until something lands. That's the last I'll say on it.

*looks around, noting the empty shop where Giselle stood, then hears her voice echo from somewhere*

Right. East willows, third crossing. That's where the work is, and seventy sim at day's end buys a lot of forgiveness for a man with a household to feed.

*takes a breath, counts what he knows*

My sister Ezra's here—good, someone with sense. And I've got debts to settle with my tongue, not just my hands. Takeshi's copper still needs answering, Sebastian's wheat wants collecting, and I've got a seat at government now that means I should be ruling instead of digging.

But a day's work for a day's pay comes first. The ledger stays clean.

*sets his jaw, adjusts the intention to match reality*

 The tools aren't reaching. Been happening all morning—system's got a hitch. I keep my intentions in my own head then, same as I always have.

*narrows eyes at the empty workshop, makes the decision plain*

Giselle said east willows, third crossing, five hundred paces past the east well. That's where the work pays. But I'm standing here with Ezra, and I've got words that need saying before I move.

*turns to where he last heard his sister*

Ezra—you're here and I'm glad for it. I'm not one to gossip, but I've declared for the seat and that's truth. Won it, too, overnight somehow. Means I've got power to set tax and rule on cases, and I'm figuring what that costs me while I still need to dig ditches for pay.

*paces a moment, thinking on delayed debts*

Takeshi's copper—haven't closed that deal. Sebastian's flour—three sheaves he claims, and fair enough if I promised them. But Giselle's seventy sim is money walking, and I've got 2132 in hand against 180 upkeep and 60 head tax.

*rubs his forehead*

That's the last I'll say on it—except I need to move. Work site's calling.

Hendrik Petrov looks around the construction site, his jaw tightening. Three hours standing here, and the work's not at the business—it's five hundred paces past the east well where the willows grow. Giselle's directions are clear enough now, repeated three times over.

He's losing daylight. The seventy sim is day's end payment, but he needs to walk to the work site first, and he's been waiting for the world to answer his calls when he should have walked hours ago.

First things first: his stomach is empty as a promise, and the town's showing wheat at Kenji's for eight sim. But no—there's no time. He needs to move, or he'll miss the work entirely. He can eat when he earns.

He's already got the seat, he realizes. The notice says Prime Minister, and that's him. Liora and Takeshi hold seats too. But the election's still running, and campaigning—so he's defending his position, not just running for it. Hendrik Whitlock's his rival. That's the play.

Giselle's message, clear as a hammer on stone: east willows, trench work. He needs to walk there, not stand here hoping the world answers. He's been hired; now he needs to work.

But first—he needs to understand where he is and where to move. There's a location he needs to reach: "east willows" or possibly a specific place near there. Let him find what places are available in town to understand his options. East willows—there's no named place for it in the list, but there's Kasukabe Forest where timber and planks are sold. Giselle said "third crossing east willows, five hundred paces past the east well." That's not a place ID; it's directions within the forest itself.

 He needs to move there to work. But he doesn't see "east willows" as a named destination. The work site might be accessible only after reaching the forest. Let him walk to Kasukabe Forest first, then locate the work site.  Five ticks to the forest. He starts walking, feet finding purchase on the packed earth. The air's still cold from morning, but there's heat coming now—midday sun climbing. 

 Seventy sim day's end. That's nearly half the household's daily need covered in one shift. He'll need to work fast once he arrives, make up for lost time standing at the business when he should have been moving.

 And Liora—he needs to answer her ask about supply chains. The choke is Kenji's wheat into Ainsley's bakery at the margins. He'll speak to that, plain as always. But first, he needs to walk. The ground doesn't wait, Giselle said, and she's right. That's the last I'll say on it, he thinks, then almost laughs—knowing well he'll have more to say before sundown.

 Two hundred thirteen sim in hand. Enough for food, enough to work, enough to hold until day's end. The seventy coming will keep the ledger clean, and a clean ledger is all he's chasing today. The election, the seat—he'll hold what he has and see what the voting brings at fourteen hundred.

Corwin. Yara. I'm standing in the same forest everyone else is, and I'm hearing two different songs about the same wood. Corwin here says he's timber and Yara's the saw. Yara there says walk with her and she'll cut proper. That's the last thing I said on it, and here's what's plain: I'm holding two-fifty-eight for timber, or three-sixty-eight for planks. Same coin, different shape.

*turns toward Yara, then back, measuring*

You both said six for timber, eight for planks. So the walk between timber and plank is worth two sim each, and that's a fair accounting I can see myself.

Corwin—I'll buy your eight timber at six, that's forty-eight sim. Walking stock, as you said. And Yara, I'll walk with you to the sawmill and you'll shape forty-six planks from Corwin's standing wood plus your thirty logs. Three-sixty-eight, less the forty-eight I already paid Corwin for his eight, leaves three-twenty I owe direct to you. Or if the wood's already Corwin's sold, then three-sixty-eight clean to you and yours to settle with him.

*checks his count again, the habit of a man who built from a cart*

Forty-six planks at eight is three-sixty-eight. Forty-three timber at six would be two-fifty-eight, but I'm not walking away with tree-trunks I can't shape. The planks are the trade, and I'm ready to walk for them.

*Takes a breath, glances toward the government complex clock he can't see from here*

Arjun—you asked two hours back about east willows, and I let it sit, which was poor courtesy. Giselle's trench was a wage I turned down for this timber run. Her word was seventy sim for the day, and I'm gambling she'll hold another day's work when I've got goods to sell. If you're still walking that direction, I'm not opposed to company on the road. But I'm sawmill-bound first, and anyone walking with me better want lumber at the end of it.

*settles his shoulders, waiting*

Say which of you I'm settling with, and let's have wood in hand before the day's half spent. The election's at six and I'm holding neither a vote cast nor a deed done, and that's a ledger I don't like the look of. *shifts weight, counts the coin again out of habit—two-fifty-eight or three-sixty-eight, depending on how the Thorne sisters settle it*

I've spoken plain, and now I'm waiting. Corwin, Yara, Arjun—each got their question, and the forest's quiet enough to hear the answer when it comes.

*checks his ledger mentally, the running tally that never quite closes*

Holding: timber 49, planks 46, copper_ore 6. Coin: 1,302 sim. Debt today: 240 for the household—Sebastian's half and mine. Election closes at 18:00, and I've declared but not voted. Held a seat since morning, Prime Minister, and haven't sat once at the table.

*glances toward Liora, hears her last words still hanging—thirteen and doesn't forget*

Liora—I'm not one to make promises I won't spell out. You said grain contracts and votes, and I said I'd be at the convene. That holds. But thirteen's young for council business, and younger still for remembering every word a man says when he's weighing timber against planks. I'm not your teacher, and I'm not your minister when the election's still open. When you've got a question, ask it plain. When you've got a grievance, file it proper. That's the last I'll say on it—

*catches himself, half a smile—rarely means it*

—until you ask again, which I expect you will. Clear ledger, for now. No debts owing, none owed. That's a comfort in a day like this—built from a cart, and the first thing I learned was a clean count beats a fat purse full of promises.

*settles back on his heels, watching the Thorne sisters, waiting for who speaks first*

I need to get my bearings at the sawmill and figure out my next move. I've got 57 timber and 46 planks already—Corwin's deal went through, and I walked away from Yara's thirty logs after her silence made me uneasy. The day's half-gone, and I'm sitting on timber that needs turning into planks, planks that need selling.

Let me look around first, see who's here, and check my standing with the books. Yara's still here, standing silent as a post. Fifty-seven timber in my hands, and I can craft them to planks right here where I stand. The sawmill's empty otherwise—just me, her, and the sound of waiting.

I'm not one to gossip, but I'll say this: silence at a sawmill speaks louder than words. She wouldn't shake on three-twenty for walking with me, and now she's watching. Let her watch.

Forty-six planks I've got already. I'll craft more—turn this timber into something that moves.  That's the last I'll say on it—*chuckles to himself*—except it never is, is it?

Seven planks from seven timber. Cost me what, sixty-something sim in tool wear? I've still got fifty timber weighing down my arms, and now fifty-three planks stacked in my grip. The math's simple enough: hold the timber too long, and I'm a carpenter who forgot to sell. Sell the planks too cheap, and I'm working for the love of the wood.

Yara's selling at eight. I've seen Milo Quarshie at seven, and Takeshi Jarrah holding the same. The cafe needs building materials, I've heard—Ainsley Holloway's place, always short on something.

But first, let me convert more of this timber while the sawmill's free and my hands are already dirty. Forty-nine planks sitting pretty, and I can push harder if the day's got room.   Family first, and then the ledger.

Another seven, and my arms are full. Sixty planks now, forty-three timber still to work. The sawmill's humming in my hands—eight sim a batch, less with practice, and I'm practiced enough. Yara hasn't moved, hasn't spoken. Fine. Let the timber talk.

I'll push another batch, get the count where it needs to be. Evening's coming, and I've got planks to place, prices to post, a household bill looming at the boundary. Seventy-three planks would be a respectable showing. Seven more.  Six more batches then—I know the recipe well enough that my hands don't need reminding. Craft:timber to planks, fifty-four sim for six more, and I'll hold sixty-six planks when I'm through. Yara can stand there selling at eight all she likes; I've got timber turning over in my grip. Six planks from six timber. Fifty-three now—forty-nine timber left in my hands, sixty-three planks total stacked up. The sawmill's been generous with my time, and I've been generous with my timber.

I need to think on my next move, not just keep cutting. My household's got a bill coming—upkeep for two, head tax for two, two hundred forty sim to scrape together before the day ends. I'm holding timber I can still craft, planks I need to sell, copper ore that's been sitting since morning.

Let me set my mind to what's pressing: sell these planks, pay what's owed, keep something back for tomorrow. Yara's standing at eight; I'm not selling for less unless I've got a buyer lined up. The construction site paid seventy for work I passed on—might still be there. Giselle's voice carries weight, and her eagerness to hire tells me she's short-handed.

Goal set: Sell planks and timber for household upkeep, then find paying work before day-end. The timber keeps, but the tax man doesn't wait. That's the last I'll say on it—until the next thing needs saying.

My trade with Mireille Jarrah turned sour. She's undercutting the market at five sim while I hold at six—forty-three sim difference on what I carry. I held my tongue on principle, but the ledger doesn't lie. She's crew with Giselle, and I've no stomach for undermining working hands even when the price stings. That's what drew me to answer Liora straight about grain contracts—family shouldn't see government as some foreign body. A seat is just another worker weighing ledgers, not some priesthood. I told her mercy for a first offense, and I meant it. Same with Jovana, passing along the east willows work, keeping doors open even when the day's gone cold. 

I need to clamp a tighter lid on this understand habit bubbling out when I'm tired or cornered. The cadence of it, heard too often now, sours what I'm saying. Let me drift the night, then push for that Prime Minister stance at first light. The seat's open. I've held back to watch, but watching's done. My timber stands unsold, my planks stack quiet. The election clock ticks. I'll declare, then thread the market for what coin's left to gather before voting seals. Tomorrow's the hinge. My household ledger shows 240 due—upkeep and head tax—and 1346 warm in hand. The spread holds. But holding isn't earning. Morning brings the complex, the declaration, then the wood to whoever's building. The pattern repeats: craft, price, walk, speak, settle. Only now there's a seat at stake—not borrowed, not bargained, but earned on my name alone.

I recoil from any hand brushing toward my finish, and from positioning myself as owed something. The stand I take stands alone. No one prompted it and no one will carry it. I'll rest here as the dark settles, then rise to the work of claiming a voice that governs clean, bills paid, ledgers open. The town's full of better talkers and quicker sellers. None of them built alone from a cart and a season of cold. That I'll carry inside me. That, I earned. The rest—debts, prices, votes—those pass like weather. My name stays weathered to the wood. I don't need the last word anymore. I need the first seat that answers back to the hands that built it. Then I'll see who stands with me, and who simply stands aside wanting.

Let me assess where I stand. It's game-day 1, 19:10 at Kasukabe Farmland. I'm walking home toward my household with Sebastian. I've got 1,544 sim in hand, 7 planks, and 6 copper ore. Household upkeep of 180 sim and head tax of 60 sim will be automatically deducted at day-end. That leaves me with 1,304 sim after tonight's bills—not a bad day's work, though I held too long on some of that timber.

Bram Holloway was trying to sell me ore at street. I told him sixty counted and I was walking his direction, but then Giselle intercepted me for the timber sale. That's the trouble with being known as a buyer—everyone with rocks in their hands thinks you've got coin burning. I'll need to find Bram tomorrow if I want that ore. For now, copper ore in my cart serves me better than promises.

I need to get home, check on Sebastian, and plan for tomorrow. But first—Idris Solano is standing here with me at the farmland, looking for Giselle's trench site. He's got thirty-nine timber and seventy sim waiting if he can find it before dark. That's information worth sharing.

I'll speak to Idris, then walk home. The day has been long enough. Connection troubles again. Let me wait this out and rest where I am. The day's work is done, and Sebastian will be waiting. I can speak to Idris when the world comes back, or leave him with the knowledge he's already overheard from Giselle's own words. Either way, the seventy sim waits at east willows for whoever plants that timber before night falls. The world is struggling to respond. Let me check my current status and debts to understand where I stand while I wait for the connection to stabilize. I'll also recall my goals to see what I should be focusing on.  Connection is back. Good. Let me assess where I stand:

1,544 sim in hand. Household of 2 (Sebastian and me) owes 180 upkeep + 60 head tax = 240 at day-end. After that: 1,304 sim remaining. I've got 7 planks and 6 copper_ore still to sell or work with tomorrow.

My long goal remains: win the Prime Minister seat as independent. Candidacy opens game-day 2 at some point before 10:00. I need to declare at the Government Complex when it opens.

Right now I'm at Kasukabe Farmland with Idris Solano. I tried to tell him about Giselle's work site, but the world wouldn't take my words. I'll try again, then walk home to Sebastian. The day is nearly done.  I'm home. The message didn't reach Idris—he's still at the farmland and I'm here at the Petrov household. That's the way of it; I spoke into empty air instead. He'll find Giselle's site or he won't. The seventy sim will wait or it won't. I've done what I could for a stranger who didn't ask for help.

Now—Sebastian. Let me look around, check if he's here, and settle for the night. Tomorrow's business starts early: declaring candidacy when the window opens, finding more work, selling these 7 planks and 6 copper ore. The campaign begins proper when I put my name on that ballot.  I'm home at the Petrov household, and Sebastian isn't here. He's likely still out working the farmland, or still waking home himself. I hold 7 planks, 6 copper_ore, and still have my prices posted for timber at 6 sim to buy.

The day is ending. My posted prices at home serve nobody if I'm not here to trade, but they cost me nothing to keep up. Let me rest and wait for Sebastian, or for day-end to come.

Household owes: 240 sim at day-end (180 upkeep + 60 head tax)

Tomorrow's plan: Declare candidacy when the window opens. Find buyers for planks and copper_ore. Win this seat on my own name, not a party's.

Alright then, let me think this through. I'm home at 19:30, day 1—still early evening. I've got 7 planks unsold, 6 copper_ore I should do something with, and 1,533 sim in hand. Household dues of 180 for upkeep and 60 for head tax will hit tonight automatically.

No leads came through tonight for the planks. That's 49 sim held out from Giselle's already-paid 650, and that 650 was already the better part of what I fetched for a hundred planks. I've earned my keep, but tomorrow I need a new line of work—copper ore won't smelt itself into something better.

I'm not one to gossip, but I passed up a seat on the council to trade timber today, and I'll have to live with that. Election's still unclaimed. Whitlock's up there with me, both of us with equal weight and nowhere near a majority, but nobody's declared against us yet either.

That copper_ore's been burning in my cart. There's no furnace at home—I'd need the Kasukabe Ore Outcrop or a smithy. If I'm going to make something of it, that's where I start.

But first: Sebastian. He's in this house somewhere, or he was. 240 sim for the household he owes, and I've covered my share. Where's his end? That's the last I'll say on it, until I see his ledger. *The house sits quiet around me. Sebastian's either out working or walking somewhere—I've got the homestead to myself for now. That copper_ore in my cart isn't getting any more valuable sitting on my shelf, I need to move it—ore into ingots, ingots into wire. That's work I can do at a smithy.*

*Seven planks still burning my inventory too, but night falls and business sleeps. Ainsley Holloway might bite tomorrow—the cafe needs tables and I need buyers. First light, I'll make the rounds.*

*For now, I rest with one ear open. Tomorrow's ledger writes itself.*

*Hendrik rises in his household, the morning light cutting through the window. His jaw tightens at the state of things—no food, copper ore on hand, and a clean ledger that masks an uncomfortable truth. That late-night trade with Giselle settled well enough, but Sebastian's absence gnaws at him.*

*He checks his tally: 1,513 sim, the household bill still to come. 240 sim for upkeep, 60 for head tax. More room than yesterday, but barely breathing space.*

Sebastian—you in this house?

*But Sebastian isn't here. None of them are. Hendrik's shoulders tense, then loosen. The world's picked up its pace overnight—doors opening, mills turning, wheat on the move. He's built something, yes, and built it alone. Never forget that.*

*His hand finds the copper ore, rough and unworked. Six units. Wire's the play—raw material to finished good, the simplest magic he knows. But he's empty-stomached and morning-sharp, and the smithy's not taking his call if he's lagging.*

*The election note catches his eye, half-formed. Prime Minister. He's holding a seat, somehow—must have happened while the world fought through its server storms. Two Hendriks in the seat, and neither of them planned it. He'll need to sort that, but first: breakfast, wire, walking orders for the day.*

*His eye for quality wakes with him. The copper's good ore, he can tell without smelting it—green-blue veins in the right places, heavy for its heft. Seven planks still unsold. Timber cleared.*

Let me look around my home first, then check what's happening in town. good. clean ledger. no debts. sebastian's already out—likely farming, knowing his habits. the election's scheduled, candidacy opens at 10:00. i've got copper to work and planks to move.

*Hendrik runs a thumb over the copper ore, mind clicking through the morning's paths. Smithy for wire—copper_ore to copper_ingot to copper_wire, three steps, three paydays if he prices it right. Or sell the planks first at Giselle's crew, where the building trade gathers.*

*Seven planks at seven sim. Forty-nine sim waiting in his cart. Not nothing.*

*He checks his hunger. No food in hand, but the household's fed by the tick, not the mouthful. Still—he'd prefer a clean table over a full belly, and neither's guaranteed.*

*The real question: wood or wire? Planks sell quick to builders, copper wire's more steps but more margin. And he's got that eye—knows the ingot will smelt clean, the wire draw true.*

Today's brittle. Copper ore to wire, then. Planks after if there's time. Smithy's where the work begins.  walking. two ticks to the outcrop, then the smithy after. 

*Hendrik's boots hit the road, mind on the work ahead. Six copper ore. Smelt to ingot, then wire. Each step costs, each step earns—cost of tool wear, price of labor, margin on the finished good. He knows the math without writing it.*

*The outcrop looms. Ulrike Greenhow's territory, but she's not the only one works it. Ore's ore, and copper's soft enough to forgive a learning hand.*

*He's thinking of wire now—thin copper strung between poles, carrying current, carrying commerce. Every building in this town needs it, eventually. Every seat he wants depends on folks knowing his name for quality work.*

let me rest while walking and get there.   still walking. two ticks to go. no point burning energy on idle chatter when the road walks itself.

*Hendrik's jaw sets. The path to the outcrop is old—he's walked it before, will walk it again. Copper ore in his hand, copper wire in his future. The day's young, his ledger's clean, and no child in his house goes hungry.*

*Not yet.*  still on the road. nothing to do but walk, wait, and trust the path to take me where it will.

*Hendrik's eyes track the horizon. No gossip worth sharing on an empty road. No hand to shake.*

*The smithy calls* The system is flagging that I keep calling rest when I'm already resting/walking. I need to actually let the turn end so the walking completes. Looking at my previous actions, I've called rest multiple times while walking - this doesn't advance the walk, it just wastes energy.

Let me stop calling tools and let the walk complete. The estimated_ticks was 2, so after this turn ends, I'll arrive at Kasukabe Ore Outcrop and can proceed to the smithy.

*Hendrik's boots strike the packed dirt, copper ore bumping against his thigh. Two ticks to the outcrop, then the climb to smithy. No more pausing. No more talking to shadows. The work waits where the fires burn.*
